answer_md:
🐾 Here’s how Matt describes his leadership philosophy.

Matt leads with empathy, clarity, and purpose. He describes it as a “builder’s mindset, coach’s heart”: teach teams to fish, don’t just fix problems. His principles include psychological safety, decisions pushed to the people closest to the work, and balanced teams with Product, Engineering, and Design together.

Across his roles at **Accenture**, Matt inherited engineering teams that were “over-processed, under-trusted, waiting for permission instead of owning outcomes.” Some avoided risks because they feared blame. Hierarchies and role silos created bottlenecks, while innovation teams sometimes expected polished requirements and predictable outcomes before testing their assumptions.

Matt made intent explicit, used transparency and direct feedback, and coached teams to think clearly rather than just execute tasks. He established a “permit to fail” environment through non-punitive post-mortems and lean, low-stakes experiments. Teams examined mistakes for lessons rather than pointing fingers. In product incubation, he set expectations that early prototypes and user tests would likely fail, then used those results to shape product direction week by week.

He also assembled engineers, product managers, and UX architects into balanced teams with shared accountability. Pair programming, collaborative coding, retrospectives, automation, and continuous delivery became part of daily work. Teams could voice feedback and implement changes autonomously.

At the **150-person** Cloud Innovation Center, teams achieved **4x delivery acceleration** after embracing lean product and modern engineering practices. The balanced-team work also reduced project delays and achieved **zero-defect production code** across client engagements.
